description:
Project Overview

Raw Timber Pergola

involved building a timber prototype in Roatán, Honduras. It uses local laurel trees and robotic fabrication as a sustainable alternative to imported building materials.

Keywords

Robotic timber construction, drone scanning, tropical architecture, micro-factory, local resource use, joinery.

Professional Role & Responsibilities

Workflow Development:

Contributed to the software stack that adjusts geometry based on the data from scanned timber.

Fabrication:

Managed the robotic workflow using two robots on tracks.

Key Technical Contributions

Material Identification

: Used drone scans to identify and incorporate tree forks and irregular segments into the structural model.

Adaptive Robotics:

Utilized a system of two industrial robots to mill and assemble the structure, completing 500 kg of timber in 50 hours of CNC time.

Hybrid Construction:

Combined robotic manufacturing with local techniques, such as traditional thatch roofing, within a mobile "micro-factory" setup.

title: Echowood

description:
Project Overview

Echowood

is a research-driven thesis project developed within the Master in Robotics and Advanced Construction (MRAC). The project addresses the ecological imperative of timber circularity by repurposing diverse waste wood streams into bespoke architectural acoustic elements. By synthesizing material science, computational acoustics, and robotic fabrication, Echowood proposes a multi-tiered system that adapts design and manufacturing methodologies to the inherent non-uniformity of reclaimed timber.

Keywords

Robotic pick-and-place, custom end-effector design, computer vision (OpenCV), robotic milling, acoustic raytracing, circular economy, digital inventorying, non-standard timber fabrication.

Professional Role & Responsibilities

Computational Design:

Developed the overarching framework for material identification, acoustic simulation, and robotic path planning.

Hardware:

Designed and prototyped a custom robotic end-effector for automated nailing and assembly processes.

Scanning and Digital Library:

Created an automated digital library system using computer vision to bridge the gap between physical waste material and digital design environments.

Key Technical Contributions

1. Digital Material Library & Computer Vision Pipeline

Developed an automated workflow to digitize non-standard waste wood.

Image Processing:

Implemented a computer vision pipeline using OpenCV to perform homography and edge detection on 2D DSLR photography.

Automated Scaling:

Engineered the system to automatically identify dimensions and scale irregular pieces, storing them in a digital inventory for real-time design allocation.

2. High-Speed Acoustic Feedback System

Integrated an agile simulation loop to inform early-stage design decisions.

Raytracing Integration:

Developed a method utilizing acoustic raytracing to provide near-instant design feedback.

Performance Optimization:

Prioritized raytracing over full acoustic simulations to maintain computational efficiency when dealing with the complex, non-uniform geometries inherent in reclaimed wood.

3. Multi-Tiered Robotic Fabrication Framework

Categorized waste streams into three distinct fabrication "tiers" based on material quality and desired acoustic performance:

Low Tier (Automated Assembly):

Utilized pallet wood processed through robotic pick-and-place and automated nailing, utilizing a custom-built end-effector developed in a workshop context.

Mid Tier (Geometric Texture):

Focused on pallet wood integration involving variable-angle cutting and strategic stacking to create intricate, sound-diffusing surface textures.

High Tier (Subtractive Refinement):

Utilized live-edge pine offcuts. These were stacked and post-processed via 6-axis robotic milling, enabling a high degree of surface design control for specific acoustic scattering requirements

---

title: Realform
excerpt: Project Overview re(al)form represents an introductory exploration into the synthesis of generative AI and robotic fabrication during the first yea...
description:
Project Overview

re(al)form

represents an introductory exploration into the synthesis of generative AI and robotic fabrication during the first year of the Master in Robotics and Advanced Construction (MRAC). The project focuses on the transformation of live-edge pine offcuts into highly bespoke architectural cladding elements. By utilizing a digital workflow to extract and accentuate natural material characteristics,

re(al)form

demonstrates how inherent wood grain patterns can be repurposed as primary design parameters and fabrication instructions.

Keywords

6-axis robotic milling, OpenCV to Stable Diffusion workflow, grain-based toolpathing, digital material scanning, bespoke façade cladding, waste minimization, vectorization.

Professional Role & Responsibilities

Computational Design:

Developed a hybrid workflow utilizing computer vision and generative models to translate physical timber features into digital vectors.

Robotic Fabrication Specialist:

Programmed and executed 6-axis milling operations designed to interact specifically with the organic topography of timber offcuts.

Material Strategy Coordinator:

Managed the edge-matching and nesting logic for irregular timber geometries to maximize material yield for façade assembly.

Key Technical Contributions

1. AI-Enhanced Grain Extraction Pipeline

Developed a sophisticated digital workflow to bridge the gap between raw material imagery and fabrication-ready data.

Hybrid Vectorization:

Implemented an OpenCV to Stable Diffusion workflow to process original photography of pine offcuts, effectively isolating and vectorizing grain patterns that are typically difficult to extract via standard edge detection.

Generative Processing:

Utilized latent diffusion models to refine and clarify the grain structure, ensuring the resulting vectors were suitable for high-precision toolpath generation.

2. Grain 6-Axis Milling

Translated organic material data into subtractive manufacturing instructions.

Accentuated Toolpaths:

Utilized the extracted grain vectors as the primary driver for 6-axis robotic milling operations, physically carving into the timber to accentuate its natural aesthetic.

Material-Informed Design:

Established a design language where the fabrication process is dictated by the unique biological growth patterns of each specific wood piece.

3. Bespoke Façade Cladding System

Engineered a functional architectural application for irregular timber offcuts.

Edge-Matching Logic:

Developed a methodology for matching the edges of non-standard pine pieces, ensuring a cohesive assembly while significantly minimizing material waste.

High-Fidelity Prototyping:

Produced a "cladding element" prototype that demonstrates the scalability of grain-driven robotic carving for large-scale architectural surfaces.

---

title: Robotic Glazing Coreography
excerpt: Robotic Glazing Choreography explores the integration of advanced technologies such as motion tracking, colour sensing, and robotic painting to rep...
description:
Robotic Glazing Choreography

explores the integration of advanced technologies such as motion tracking, colour sensing, and robotic painting to replicate the hand gestures of traditional ceramic glazing craftsmanship.

---

Robotic Glazing Choreography

explores the integration of advanced technologies such as motion tracking, colour sensing, and robotic painting to replicate the hand gestures of traditional ceramic glazing craftsmanship.

---

​​​​​​​To address global challenges, the AEC industry increasingly draws inspiration from traditional techniques, linked to territories and sustainable materials. Ceramics, in particular, stand  out as a material that continues to evolve alongside modern technologies while preserving time honoured fabrication methods. This enduring versatility has sparked growing interest among  architects and designers, as ceramics serve diverse purposes—from objects to facade cladding, roof  tiling, and floor paving. Furthermore, the combination of clay sculpting and glazing provides  extensive opportunities for customisation, offering both rich materiality and lasting durability. These  attributes align seamlessly with Heatherwick Studio’s Humanise campaign.

However, replicating the precision, refinement, and tactile quality of artisanal ceramic craftsmanship  at an industrial scale remains a significant challenge for the construction industry. The “Robotic  Glazing Choreography” workshop aims to bridge that gap by studying traditional glazing  techniques—such as brushing and dropping—and translating them into a digital and robotic process,  preserving the artistry while leveraging modern technology. This dual approach would provide  participants with a comprehensive understanding of both methodologies and how they can coexist  and complement each other.

title: Forested
description:
Project Overview

The

FORESTED

project represents a sophisticated inquiry into the intersection of computational design, robotic fabrication, and sustainable timber management. The primary objective is the high-value transformation of non-standard, organic wood geometries—specifically beech forks and live-edge oak and birch—into functional architectural elements through advanced digital manufacturing workflows.

Keywords

3/6-axis robotic milling, toolpath optimization, stack lamination, computational design, design-to-manufacturing workflows, digital fabrication, robotic joinery, live-edge processing.

Professional Role & Responsibilities

Lead of Computational Pretotypes:

Directed the development and execution of technical prototypes, specifically focusing on complex timber geometries.

Fabrication Strategy Coordination:

Managed the integration of 3-axis CNC and 6-axis industrial robotics to resolve the unique constraints of irregular wood species.

Key Technical Contributions

1. Robotic Column Fabrication (Beech Fork Integration)

Developed a complete computational pipeline for the structural joining of natural beech forks.

6-Axis Milling:

Executed robotic milling to create high-precision joinery, allowing two organic forks to be stacked vertically into a singular, structural column.

Geometry Reconciliation:

Utilized computational tools to reconcile the natural variances of the forks with the requirements of robotic path planning.

2. Live-Edge Oak Parquet System

Engineered a specialized flooring solution utilizing live-edge oak.

CNC Processing: Employed 3-axis CNC milling to process the oak while maintaining the organic "live edge" aesthetic.

Standardization vs. Variation:

Implemented a workflow that allows for functional floor installation while preserving the inherent material character.

3. Parametric Birch Dividing Wall

Designed and fabricated a parametric partition using live-edge birch slabs.

Optimized Toolpaths: Developed specific toolpath strategies to manage the material behaviour and fabrication tolerances of birch.

---

title: Micro House
excerpt: Project Overview The 3D printed Micro house
description:
Project Overview

The

3D printed Micro house

is a competition entry for Buildner that explores the intersection of robotic earth construction and sustainable off-grid living. The project addresses the global housing crisis and the high carbon footprint of the building industry by utilizing 3D earth printing to create a durable, biodegradable, and accessible micro-home. The design prioritizes comfort and "small luxuries" within a minimal footprint, demonstrating that off-grid living can be both sustainable and high-quality.

Keywords

3D earth printing, robotic additive manufacturing, passive design, thermal mass, off-grid systems, embodied carbon reduction, biodegradable materials, micro-housing.

Professional Role & Responsibilities

Collaborative Designer & Researcher:

Developed the conceptual framework for robotic earth construction in a remote context.

Sustainability Strategist: Integrated passive design principles to reduce operational energy loads and managed the selection of low-carbon, natural materials.

Computational Design Contributor: Assisted in the development of self-shading wall geometries and structural forms optimized for additive manufacturing.

Key Technical Contributions

1. Additive Manufacturing with Natural Materials

The project utilizes robotic 3D printing to process earth-based mixtures into structural wall systems.

Material Circularity: Proposed the use of locally sourced soil to minimize transport-related emissions and ensure the structure is fully biodegradable at the end of its lifecycle.

Geometry Optimization: Developed wall forms that leverage the precision of robotic extrusion to create complex, self-supporting structures without the need for traditional formwork.

2. Passive Environmental Design

The architectural form is driven by environmental performance to maintain internal comfort without active mechanical systems.

Thermal Mass & Self-Shading: Engineered wall geometries that provide high thermal mass for temperature regulation and integrated self-shading patterns to mitigate solar heat gain.

3. Integrated Off-Grid Systems

The design functions as a self-sustaining unit through the management of water and energy resources.

Operational Efficiency: By combining passive design with site-specific orientation, the home minimizes energy demand for heating and cooling, supporting a comfortable off-grid lifestyle.

title: Subtractive Milling Strategies
excerpt: Keywords 3/6-axis robotic milling, toolpath optimization, stack lamination, computational design, design-to-manufacturing workflows, digital fabric...
description:
Keywords

3/6-axis robotic milling, toolpath optimization, stack lamination, computational design, design-to-manufacturing workflows, digital fabrication

Role & Responsibilities

Development and coordination of a one-week intensive workshop focused on optimized design-to-fabrication workflows for stack lamination using 3- and 6-axis robotic milling.

Support and instruction of students enrolled in the Master in Robotics and Advanced Construction and the Master in Ecological Buildings, with emphasis on computational design strategies, fabrication constraints, and hands-on operation of industrial robotic systems.

Key Contributions

- Designed and implemented a complete design-to-manufacturing pipeline, integrating computational design tools with robotic fabrication processes.

- Developed optimized toolpath strategies for multi-axis milling, balancing precision, material efficiency, machining time, and surface quality.

- Led hands-on training sessions on robotic setup, calibration, tool selection, and finishing techniques for laminated timber assemblies.

- Provided technical guidance on stack lamination logic, material behaviour, and fabrication tolerances across different wood species.

- Supported students in translating conceptual design intent into fabrication-ready geometries, ensuring feasibility within robotic and material constraints.

---

CNC milling

is widely applied in manufacturing for precision parts, furniture production, prototyping, and standardized workflows where speed and accuracy are prioritized.

Similarly,

robotic milling

offers higher precision, repeatability, and the ability to produce complex geometries that would be time-intensive or impossible by hand. However, it lacks the intuitive, adaptive knowledge of a craftsperson and requires upfront digital planning.

It is most effective for large-scale components, non-standard geometries, and processes requiring flexibility in tool orientation. Designing for robotic milling involves anticipating material behaviour, tool accessibility, and integrating robotic constraints into the design from the start.

---

To address these challenges and opportunities, this workshop explored a hybrid workflow combining 3-axis CNC milling and 6-axis robotic milling. A 3-axis CNC machine was first employed

to produce the rough contours of a geometry through the stacking of plywood layers, approximating the desired form. This stage focused on understanding toolpath generation, material efficiency, and geometric translation from digital to physical form.

In the second phase, a 6-axis robotic milling process was used to perform finishing operations on the assembled piece. By taking advantage of the robot’s full kinematic range, including its external rotary axis, the surface geometry was refined to achieve smooth, continuous forms that would be difficult to produce with conventional methods. This phase emphasized the robotic toolpath planning, calibration, and adaptive machining strategies.
